title: Water physics
author: That1guy4226
selftext: I have been trying to get this water to look and flow right but I just cant seem to get it past this point. Has anyone else has any luck with this type of water simulation?

replies.author: That1guy4226
replies.body: Working on a game similar to Turmoil but for gold panning. It has a 3d river and campsite that you upgrade.

comments.author: junmakesgames
comments.body: what method are you using here? are you aiming for real time?

replies.author: That1guy4226
replies.body:
I’m using a hybrid real-time approach rather than a full physics simulation. The player’s mouse movement is analyzed for tilt, speed, circular motion, and movement toward the rim. Those inputs drive gameplay values for separation, sediment washout, and possible gold loss.

Visually, the water uses a lightweight container-fluid simulation, while the sediment and gold are repositioned using scripted rules and shaders. The goal is real-time interaction, but with an approximation that looks and feels believable without the performance cost of simulating everything. I may just end up doing that anyways but idk

replies.author: junmakesgames
replies.body: what's the container fluid simulation you're using? i imagine you can definitely just get by with one way coupling of the bowl and the sediment ( is that the big brown thing) as boundary conditions to the fluid simulation if you aren't already doing that

replies.author: That1guy4226
replies.body: Its a custom built sim. And yeah that is the current sediment. I need to give the slurry grid several more material layers. I kinda got ahead of myself and have realized I am trying to solve this issue a bit too soon. This did push me down the right path though thanks.

replies.author: junmakesgames
replies.body: i understand it's custom built haha i'm just curious what numerical method you're using or anything that can help me understand what you're doing

replies.author: That1guy4226
replies.body:
It’s a simplified explicit finite-volume shallow-water solver on a 2D heightfield. The pan interior is discretized into a 31×31 grid. Each cell stores water volume, and velocities are stored on the faces between neighboring cells.

For each timestep, I calculate face acceleration from the local gravity vector plus the difference in neighboring free-surface heights:

`a ≈ g_planar - g_normal × surface_gradient`

I integrate the face velocities explicitly, apply exponential damping and a velocity limit, then calculate the volume flux across each face:

`flux = velocity × wetted_depth × face_width × dt`

The outgoing fluxes are scaled when necessary so a cell can never send more water than it contains. That gives me conservative transport and stable wet/dry cells without negative water volumes. The simulation uses fixed substeps no larger than 1/120 second.

Spilling is handled at exposed rim cells with a simple weir-style discharge approximation proportional to `head^(3/2)`, where `head` is the water surface above the rim.

The sediment is one-way coupled by adding its mound shape to the solver’s floor-height field. That displaces water and changes the crests and flow paths between cells, but fluid forces are not fed back into a granular solver.

So it’s not a full Navier–Stokes/SPH/FLIP simulation, and it doesn’t use a formal Riemann solver. It’s closer to a lightweight staggered-grid, finite-volume shallow-water approximation designed for stable real-time container sloshing.

That is the AIs explanation just to be clear.

replies.author: junmakesgames
replies.body:
got it! shallow water solver!  i kind of figured it was an ai implementation when you called it a container method. 🤣

i think this looks great and is a cool usage of shallow water. one thing  i'm curious about is why when the problem initializes when everything is axi symmetric (when the mound is centered and there's no tilt yet) and in equilibrium, why is the free surface solution not flat? is that some noise you're adding to get some of those water stretching at the outer radius?

replies.author: That1guy4226
replies.body:
It isn’t intentional noise. The water starts flat using the empty pan shape, and then the sediment mound is added as a boundary. That pushes the water surface upward, so the solver needs time to settle it back to level. The roughness around the outer edge is mostly stair-stepping from the relatively coarse 31×31 grid.

I really appreciate the help and insight. I don’t have a technical background, so I’ve been amazed by what someone like me can build with the tools available now. The whole experience has honestly been a little mind-blowing.
